bridge: Builds on F01 root causes, C06 page permissions and S01 layered controls.
teaching:
A mitigation makes some exploitation paths harder or detects some faults; it does not necessarily eliminate the underlying bug. Address randomisation changes layout predictability. Non-executable memory restricts where instructions execute. Stack canaries detect certain stack overwrites before a protected return path. Each has a specific scope.

A bounds-safe or memory-safe design addresses a different layer by preventing invalid access under its language/runtime guarantees. Unsafe escapes, foreign-function interfaces and logic flaws still need review. Avoid treating a language name as a complete system proof.

Evaluate defences against the same threat scenario so the comparison is meaningful. State what data an attacker controls, where corruption occurs and what check runs before a harmful action. Regression tests should verify repaired behaviour as well as the presence of a build flag. A flag appearing in a configuration file is not proof it applied to the deployed binary.

Data-execution prevention/NX and W^X are related but different: NX marks a mapping non-executable, whereas W^X is a policy against simultaneous write-and-execute permissions. A JIT may transition a page from writable to executable under a controlled protocol. Neither policy repairs an out-of-bounds write. Code-reuse attacks try to redirect control through existing executable instructions rather than injecting new instructions; this is why NX alone is incomplete. Effective ASLR depends on which mappings are randomised, usable entropy and leaks; do not infer protection solely from a flag name. Build defaults change, so inspect the actual target artifact and configuration.

A mitigation may stop a particular control-flow hijack while leaving other damage possible. A crash can occur after data has leaked or a transaction has changed state; it is also a loss of availability. Memory-safe application code can still depend on unsafe native libraries, runtimes, foreign-function interfaces or deliberately unsafe blocks. Explain the boundary of the guarantee rather than promising that one language makes the whole system secure. Page permissions constrain execution and writes at page granularity; they do not check the bounds of each C object.
example:
Fault: write9 bytes into an8-byte object.
Bounds check: rejects before write -> addresses root cause.
NX: may block execution from a data page -> write can still corrupt data.
ASLR: changes addresses -> does not make9 fit into8.
Canary: may detect some overwrites -> layout/path dependent.
Memory-safe container: enforces bounds under its supported operations.
explanation: The key arithmetic remains wrong under all layout mitigations. Data-only corruption may matter even when injected code cannot execute. A useful report explains the remaining consequence rather than dismissing a bug because one exploit technique is harder.
exercise: Create a table for the four controls above: prevention/detection/hardening role, assumption and one remaining risk. Add a verification step that checks actual build/runtime behaviour for a selected mitigation without attempting an exploit.
solution: Bounds checking can prevent the invalid write; NX/ASLR harden consequences; canaries detect selected patterns. Verification may inspect the built artifact or runtime mapping using the assigned tools, with platform/version recorded.
challenge: A reviewer says “ASLR is enabled, so the overflow is fixed.” Write a precise response and propose both a source repair and a boundary regression test.
challenge_solution: ASLR does not repair the out-of-bounds operation. Check required capacity before copying or use a representation that enforces bounds; test just-below, exact-fit and over-limit input while preserving ordinary successful use.
